articles.title: Planning permission granted for MoD Bicester asylum centre plans
articles.summary: The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the site near Bicester was fast-tracked.
articles.body:
Planning permission to house asylum seekers at a former military site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington has been granted by the government.

The Home Office's application to house up to 1,256 men at the MoD Bicester site was fast-tracked using an Urgent Crown Development application.

The nearby village of Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK in opposition to the planned site, which has also been legally challenged by campaigners.

A Home Office spokesperson said the planning permission "allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester" but no final decision on the proposal had been taken.

A government report said the decision received 3,177 representations against, and one in support.

It also said Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ruled permission should be granted because "national demand for asylum accommodation remains high".

The permission allows for demolition of existing buildings, the erection of new modular accommodation, and provisions for health and welfare facilities.

Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, said: "Angela Rayner and the Labour government have betrayed the people of Piddington by abusing their emergency powers in this way."

He continued: "Instead of accommodating illegal immigrants, the government should leave the ECHR so they can be rapidly deported."

Lib Dem MP for Bicester and Woodstock Calum Miller said it was "the wrong plan and the wrong site for local communities, asylum seekers and taxpayers".

"I am deeply disappointed that the government has approved this proposal despite the serious concerns raised by residents and local councils as well as the major problems with the site," he added.

The approval could be challenged by an application to the High Court within six weeks, beginning with the day after the date of the decision.

The government said a challenge "may be brought only on the ground that the decision is legally flawed; it is not an opportunity to reconsider the planning merits".

Joe Marshall, a Piddington parish councillor, said residents of the village were "extremely frustrated".

"The government has approved its own application against more than 3,000 objections and one letter of support, overruling the councils, the NHS and the Police and Crime Commissioner," he said.

He told BBC Newsnight: "This development is something that nobody would want to have imposed on their local area."

Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said: "Over 1,200 unvetted illegal migrant men are being dumped in Piddington.

"Tory and Labour governments have betrayed their own people. Reform will detain and deport all of these men."

A Home Office spokesperson said: "A final decision to proceed is yet to be taken.

"The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1 billion saved in costs since the election.

"This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

"These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community."

articles.title: New Jersey couple report seeing 8-foot tall Bigfoot stepping out in front of their car: 'We know what we saw'
articles.summary: A New Jersey couple claims an 8-foot creature covered in jet-black fur crossed the road in front of their car on a rainy October night in the state.
articles.body: A New Jersey couple deemed to be credible witnesses by the investigators who met with them say a Bigfoot, roughly 8-feet tall, crossed the road in front of them while they were driving on a rainy Sunday night around 10:30 p.m. in October. The husband and wife "had a very normal, human reaction to seeing something they didn't believe exists," BFRO investigator Jacob Korbel reported. Following their encounter, they called the NJ State Park Police and the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS As the wife was driving with her husband and kids, she says she became terrified. The car's high beams had caught a glimpse of a massive figure stepping out in front of their vehicle on what she described as a rural road. She slowed down and reported that this massive figure stood about 8-feet tall. "It was bulky, heavily built GIANT frame. It was covered in jet-black fur and it appeared to be soaking wet. Our headlights were reflecting off its fur. I saw enough detail to distinguish human-like hands and unusually long arms," she claims. "It walked with a slight hunch but moved at fast speed. It didn’t take many steps for it to get across the road. Thing moved fast enough to look like it was gliding without actually gliding. Its arms swung like a human walks but with heavy reach. I asked my husband if he was seeing the same thing I was ... He confirmed that he saw it." articles.title: London court finds 2 Iranian men guilty of spying for Iran
articles.summary: LONDON — Two Iranian men who spied on journalists working for a Persian-language broadcaster in London were found guilty Thursday of spying for Iran.
articles.body: LONDON — Two Iranian men who spied on journalists working for a Persian-language broadcaster in London were found guilty Thursday of spying for Iran. Following a six-week trial at Woolwich Crown Court in south London, Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The IRGC was outlawed by the U.K. in July under new powers to counteract state threats, with penalties of up to 14 years in prison for anyone convicted of supporting or assisting the organization. A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was acquitted on all charges. “This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime,” said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counter-terrorism division. He said the pair were promised rewards in exchange for sending intelligence back to Iran, while Sepahvand was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit serious violence against their targets. These included journalists for Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner. Iran International is banned by the government in Tehran. London’s Metropolitan Police said this was the fourth case in recent years involving a direct threat to Iran International journalists and that it is “working hard to keep them safe.” “The threat from hostile states to the U.K. is increasing and Iran continues to adapt its approach to using ‘proxies’,” said Vicki Evans, a deputy assistant commissioner at the London police. “We have seen examples of people who fly into the country to carry out criminal activity and then leave shortly afterwards, to using British nationals or, in this case, Iranian nationals with settled immigration status,” she added. Counterterrorism police have looked into the possible involvement of Iranian proxies in a series of recent incidents, particularly attacks on the Jewish community in London, including the arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances earlier this year that many said was a direct result of the start of the Iran war. Most recently, Iran has been linked with a plot against a U.S.-run military air base in England. The Iranian Embassy in the U.K. has said that it “categorically rejects” allegations of involvement in “violent activities or incidents in the United Kingdom.” Sepahvand and Manesh were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. “Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place,” prosecutor Ferguson said. The pair will be sentenced at London’s Central Criminal Court, better known as the Old Bailey, on Dec. 17.

articles.title: A woman booked a Washington Airbnb for 32 days after a fire displaced her, but stayed for months; the homeowner offered $2,500 and two months of free rent before a judge ruled in her favour
articles.summary: A short-term rental arrangement can become complicated when a guest decides not to leave after the agreed period.
articles.body: A short-term rental arrangement can become complicated when a guest decides not to leave after the agreed period. That is what happened to Rochanne Douglas, a Washington, D.C., homeowner who initially welcomed a woman into her Northeast Washington property for a 32-day Airbnb stay. The booking was supposed to provide temporary accommodation while the guest waited for repairs to her previous apartment. Instead, the arrangement stretched into several months, payments became irregular and the guest disputed the homeowner’s attempts to regain possession. Even an offer of $2,500, alongside two months without rent, did not bring an immediate end to the disagreement. The matter eventually reached a judge.How a 32-day Airbnb booking turned into an extended stay in a Washington rowhouseAs reported by The Washington Post, the arrangement began in late February 2025 when Shadija Romero booked Douglas’s Northeast Washington rowhouse through Airbnb. Douglas, 49, had owned the property since 2019 and was working as a realtor and entrepreneur in Maryland.Romero reportedly explained that a fire had forced her out of her previous apartment and that repairs would take slightly more than a month. She wanted somewhere to stay while the work was completed. Douglas agreed to accommodate her, charging $100 a night through Airbnb.The initial booking covered 32 days. Romero made the payments through the platform and moved into the property expecting a temporary arrangement. When the agreed period ended, however, she asked to remain for another month. She said the repairs at her previous accommodation were taking longer than expected. Reportedly, this time, the payments were made directly to Douglas rather than through Airbnb.The change in arrangement would later become an important part of the dispute. Airbnb subsequently clarified that the extended stay was covered by a separate agreement between the homeowner and Romero, not by the original platform booking.Late payments and past eviction records raised concerns for the homeownerAccording to Douglas, Romero initially kept up with the payments. The situation began changing around June, when payments started arriving late or in smaller amounts. Romero also requested additional time to settle what she owed.Douglas said she began looking into Romero's background through public court records after the repeated payment problems. Her searches uncovered previous landlord-tenant disputes, including a substantial unpaid rent balance connected to another District apartment.Court records reviewed by The Washington Post showed that Romero owed nearly $50,000 in back rent for an apartment in Washington, D.C., in 2024. She had also been ordered evicted from another District apartment building in 2023 over unpaid rent. Public records showed at least a dozen judgments or liens involving her dating back to 2008, most relating to landlord-tenant matters in Maryland and Virginia.By August, Douglas had become increasingly concerned about the arrangement. When the payment for that month had still not arrived by the middle of the month, Romero asked for another extension. Douglas responded by issuing notices asking her to leave, including an immediate vacate notice and a separate 30-day notice. Romero eventually paid the August charges, but the following month brought another round of delayed payments and installments.The homeowner's attempts to get her property backBy September, Douglas said she no longer wanted to continue the rental arrangement. After receiving the month's payment in installments, she again told Romero to vacate the property. She also warned that the electricity would be disconnected if she remained beyond October 15.Douglas said, “I told her she needed to vacate the property. And I specifically told her this is why I’m not a landlord because this is the kind of correspondence I don’t want to do.”“Airbnb is very clear. You book it, they pay you the next day. ... I didn’t want to be in a situation where I had to listen to this every month.”Douglas maintained that she did not want to continue accepting payments or extend the arrangement. Her position was that the original short-term booking had ended and there was no agreement for Romero to remain indefinitely.When October 15 arrived without Romero leaving, Douglas arranged for the electricity to be switched off. But the power was restored shortly afterwards. According to Douglas, Romero had transferred the electricity account with Pepco, the local utility provider, into her own name and arranged for the service to resume. Romero's position was that she had tenant rights and could not simply be removed from the property. That argument brought a separate legal complication into the dispute.Under Washington, D.C.'s tenant protections, a written lease is not always necessary for a tenancy to exist. However, landlords can pursue eviction for unpaid rent through the required legal process after giving the appropriate notice.Airbnb also distanced itself from the extended stay. A company spokesperson told The Washington Post, “This agreement was separate from any prior booking made through Airbnb. While issues like this are rare, hosts and guests should always communicate, book, and pay on Airbnb, so they’re covered by our policies and protections.”Homeowner offered $2,500 and waived two months' rent, but Airbnb guest refused to leaveWith the disagreement continuing, Douglas consulted a lawyer about her options. She was advised that Washington, D.C.'s housing laws could allow Romero to delay an eviction for months. Douglas then proposed a settlement intended to avoid a prolonged court battle. Under the agreement, Romero would leave the property by November 15 and give up any claim to tenancy rights. In exchange, Douglas agreed not to charge her for October or November. She also offered an additional $2,500 to help with relocation expenses.Romero signed the document on October 23, and it was submitted to the court. The November deadline passed without the property being vacated. Douglas said she then took a copy of the signed agreement to the police and asked officers to help remove Romero.The homeowner's efforts to regain possession continued to encounter difficulties. When Douglas arrived at the house with police, Romero again maintained that she was a tenant and refused to leave. Douglas said she told Romero that she could not continue allowing someone to occupy the property without paying. She also pointed to her monthly mortgage payment of approximately $4,000, which continued to be her responsibility.The dispute grew beyond the original payment disagreement. Douglas alleged that Romero had disabled security cameras at the property and contacted authorities to have Douglas's car towed from the driveway. Douglas eventually put up a large red-and-white notice on the front of the house declaring that the occupant was unauthorised. Romero covered part of the sign with a sheet, although it remained visible.Police visits and a temporary return to the propertyThe situation appeared to be nearing an end just before Thanksgiving, when Douglas received word from neighbours that Romero seemed to have moved out. The following morning, Douglas returned to the property with police officers. She said the house was empty and that officers told her she could change the locks and secure the building. She removed the batteries from the electronic locks and arranged for contractors to board up the property. The electricity and water were also disconnected. Douglas said police had informed her that Romero could face arrest for breaking and entering if she returned.A few days later, neighbours contacted Douglas again, reporting that Romero had returned to the house with police. According to Douglas, officers allowed Romero to remove the locks and enter the property again. The homeowner was back in the same position, with the disagreement still unresolved. On December 4, an emergency virtual court hearing resulted in an order requiring Douglas to restore electricity and water to the house while the wider case was being considered.A judge ruled that the signed agreement gave up the tenancy claimThe case eventually reached D.C. Superior Court, where Judge Maurice Ross heard evidence from Douglas, her lawyer and Romero. The judge focused on the agreement Romero had signed on October 23. The document required her to leave by November 15 and acknowledged that she did not have tenant rights. By signing it, Ross determined Romero had given up her claim to tenancy. The judge therefore allowed Douglas to retake possession of the property without waiting through the usual 20-day period.He told the homeowner that she could begin the process immediately. The ruling was welcomed by D.C. Council member Zachary Parker, who represents Ward 5, where the property is located. Parker said he was pleased that the court had brought the dispute towards a resolution and that his team would examine District laws to understand how the situation had been allowed to develop. A representative from the D.C. The Office of the Tenant Advocate said that short-term rental regulations were designed, among other things, to protect the supply of housing intended for longer-term residents.The homeowner finally regained control of the houseDouglas moved quickly after the judge's decision. On Thursday afternoon, she returned with her husband, along with friends and family members, to remove Romero's belongings from the property. The items included candles, books, bedding, towels, electronic equipment and kitchenware. They were placed in the driveway behind the house as the homeowner worked to recover possession.Romero later posted an emotional video on TikTok, disputing aspects of the account that had circulated about her stay and the unpaid payments. She challenged the suggestion that she had remained in the property since February without making payments after March, saying that this version of events was untrue. She also addressed the criticism directed towards her following the court ruling and said she intended to take some time for herself.According to Douglas, Romero returned to the property later that Thursday evening and collected her belongings using a U-Haul van. The two women had not spoken since.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available reports. The Times of India has not independently verified all claims, statements, payment details or circumstances surrounding the Airbnb booking and subsequent occupancy dispute. Allegations and accounts attributed to the homeowner or guest have been presented as reported and should not be interpreted as independently established facts.You use AI every day. articles.title: Rajasthan SSR draft counts 1  1  L more voters than SIR list
articles.summary: JAIPUR: Rajasthan's latest draft electoral roll, published Thursday under the Special Summary Revision (SSR) 2027, has produced a fresh numbers puzzle.
articles.body: JAIPUR: Rajasthan's latest draft electoral roll, published Thursday under the Special Summary Revision (SSR) 2027, has produced a fresh numbers puzzle. It records about 5.26 crore voters - about 11 lakh more than the 5.15 crore in the final Special Intensive Revision (SIR) roll published in Feb.But the number is still far below another official figure in circulation: State Election Commission's final electoral roll, which stood at 5.45 crore voters in early Oct.That leaves Rajasthan with three voter counts in less than a year - 5.15 crore in the final SIR roll, 5.45 crore in the SEC roll, and now 5.26 crore in the ECI-linked SSR draft. The latest figure sits between the two, but does not settle the central question: why official rolls for the same state show such wide variation. According to Chief Electoral Officer Naveen Mahajan, the SSR draft has 2,75,24,780 male voters, 2,51,42,052 female voters and 584 transgender voters. The qualifying date for the revision is Jan 1, 2027. EC has opened claims and objections from Nov 12 to Dec 11. The final roll will be published on Jan 4, 2027.The difference between SIR and SSR is critical to understanding the numbers. SIR is a deeper verification exercise in which booth-level officers conduct house-to-house enumeration. Existing voters are given pre-filled forms and are required to submit them for their names to be considered in the revised roll.SSR begins with the last published final roll. Existing voters are generally carried forward and not required to prove eligibility afresh merely to retain their names. The exercise is meant to update the roll through additions, deletions and corrections.Changes in Raj rolls can be sought till JanThis difference in method explains why a draft SSR roll may not mirror a final SIR roll. But the wider problem is the coexistence of sharply different official numbers. The SSR draft is around 11 lakh higher than the final SIR roll, yet around 18 lakh lower than the SEC’s early-Oct roll.The draft rolls have been shared with recognised political parties and uploaded on the CEO website. Voters can seek inclusion, deletion or correction through the prescribed forms before the final roll is frozen in January.Mahajan urged eligible citizens to verify their names in the draft roll and apply for inclusion if their names are missing. Those completing 18 years by Jan 1, 2027, can apply for enrolment. Young citizens turning 18 by Oct 1, 2027, can also submit advance applications.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indians top again: 9.3L get OECD citizenships in 5 years
articles.summary: Indians continue to top the list of people acquiring citizenship in advanced economies, with around 9.25 lakh Indian citizens acquiring the nationality of
articles.body: Indians continue to top the list of people acquiring citizenship in advanced economies, with around 9.25 lakh Indian citizens acquiring the nationality of an OECD member country between 2020 and 2024, according to the 'International Migration Outlook - 2026' report released on Thursday by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), reports Lubna Kably.The figure marks a sharp increase of 41% from just over 6.5 lakh Indians who acquired citizenship of OECD member countries during 2015-2019. India remains the largest country of former nationality among those acquiring citizenship in OECD member countries, ahead of Syria and Mexico.OECD countries took nearly 87L new citizens during 2020-2024India remains ahead of Syria and Mexico. whose nationals accounted for around 5.9 lakh citizenships in OECD countries each during the five-year period 2020–2024.Interestingly, while China was the sixth largest source country whose nationals acquired OECD member country citizenship, the numbers fell by nearly 12% to 3.4 lakh in 2020-24 as compared to the previous five-year period. OECD comprises 38 member countries – notably US, UK, European nations, Australia, Canada, Japan and South Korea.According to additional data shared with TOI, during 2020-2024, OECD member countries embraced nearly 87 lakh new citizens – Indians constitute around 10% of its new citizens. In the previous five-year period, nearly 65 lakh individuals acquired citizenship of an OECD member country – once again the composition of Indians was 10%.OECD also shared year-on-year India-specific data with TOI, showing that 2.3 lakh Indians acquired citizenship of OECD member countries in 2024, mainly in Canada (87,320), US (48,820) and Australia (28,969). In 2023, the overall India-figure was marginally lower at nearly 2.2 lakh, with the same three countries accounting for most of the citizenship acquisitions.The latest figures underline the growing permanence of Indian migration to advanced economies. While immigration flows measure the number of people moving to another country, citizenship acquisitions offer an indication of how many immigrants have progressed to acquiring the nationality of their destination country.Indians also continued to move to OECD member countries for work and study, although the pace of migration slowed. India remained the largest origin country of new migrants to OECD member countries in 2024. However, the number of Indian-origin migrants moving to OECD member countries fell by 19% in 2024, from 6.1 lakh in 2023 to 4.9 lakh in 2024.“Migration remains high, and immigrants now account for 16% of employment across the OECD,” Mathias Cormann, OECD secretary-general said. “With ageing populations and slower productivity growth, countries cannot afford to waste the skills migrants bring. That means helping migrants move into jobs where they can contribute most, and giving immigrant entrepreneurs better access to finance, networks and business support,” he added.One in five STEM graduates across OECD member countries is foreign-born, and immigrants are over-represented among researchers and founders of innovative firms. Yet immigrants are also more likely to work in lower-productivity sectors, with their skills often underutilised, states OECD. The report finds that immigrant’s contribution to productivity depends on how effectively countries make use of their skills – many countries have expanded programmes to attract highly skilled workers. The gap between Indian and Chinese students studying in OECD member countries narrowed, with 8.3 lakh Indian students and 8.5 lakh Chinese students studying in these countries.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: A Nantucket homeowner has been accused of cutting down more than 16 mature trees on a neighbour’s property to improve the ocean view from his own home.
articles.body: A Nantucket homeowner has been accused of cutting down more than 16 mature trees on a neighbour’s property to improve the ocean view from his own home. Patricia R. Belford, trustee of the Belford Family Trust, filed a civil complaint against Jonathan Jacoby in Nantucket Superior Court on June 23, 2025. The dispute concerns land at 1 Tautemo Way. The trees had been planted by the family in the 1970s.According to a complaint filed in Nantucket Superior Court on June 23, 2025, Jacoby entered the property on or about February 22, 2025, without permission and cut down the trees. The filing says they provided privacy, shade, and a buffer from road noise. Belford is seeking compensatory and statutory damages, including treble damages, as well as relief for alleged emotional distress.Complaint alleges homeowner cut down more than 16 trees on neighbour’s landThe complaint alleges that Jacoby entered the Belford Property on or about February 22, 2025, and cut down more than 16 mature trees without notice or permission from Belford.It says he crossed the driveway before reaching the south or southwest portion of the land, where the trees were located. The filing identifies the trees as cedar, cherry, and Leyland Cypress, many of which were over 30 feet in height and decades old.It states that they formed a natural barrier between the home and Hummock Pond Road. According to the complaint, the trees also provided shade, aesthetic value, privacy, and noise mitigation.How did the homeowner allegedly benefit from removing his neighbour’s treesThe complaint claims Jacoby cut the trees to improve the ocean view from his home at 3 Tautemo Way. It says he listed that property for sale with a description promoting its ‘sweeping view of the Atlantic Ocean’. According to the filing, that wording had not appeared in earlier listings.Belford alleges Jacoby did not obtain written or verbal consent from her or anyone authorised to act for the trust. The complaint says the trees had been planted by the Belford family in the 1970s and maintained for nearly five decades.It states that their removal eliminated the property’s only natural buffer to Hummock Pond Road and left the home exposed to the street.What did police find after investigating the alleged tree cuttingThe complaint says the property manager discovered the damage and contacted the Nantucket Police Department. It identifies Officer George Haddad as the investigator and refers to a statement from Jacoby’s former landscaper, Krasimir Kirilov.In the statement included with the filing, Kirilov, of Challenge Landscaping, said in a recorded statement that Jacoby had cut down the trees. The complaint states that police gathered photographs and damage assessments and concluded Jacoby knowingly entered the property and cut the trees for personal benefit. It adds that an associated criminal proceeding remained active when the civil complaint was filed. The police report was numbered 25-002014, according to the complaint.Complaint puts tree replacement cost above $486,000The complaint cites an estimate from Surfing Hydrangea Nursery for one comparable Leyland Cypress measuring at least 30 feet tall. The estimate put the cost to purchase and transport one comparable Leyland Cypress of at least 30 feet at $22,114.06. It did not include planting or installation costs, which the complaint says would require a specialised contractor.The filing states that replacement costs for the removed trees alone exceeded $486,000. It also claims the loss reduced the property’s value and character and increased exposure to road noise, light and loss of privacy. Belford seeks compensatory and treble damages, emotional-distress and punitive damages, and an order barring Jacoby from trespassing.Disclaimer: This article is based on a civil complaint filed in Nantucket Superior Court on June 23, 2025. The Times of India has not independently verified the allegations, the circumstances surrounding the removal of the trees, or the estimated replacement costs mentioned in the complaint. The claims have not been established as findings of the court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Learn it the hard way’: Why Chinese parents are paying thousands for ‘hardship camps’ for their children to learn important life skills
articles.summary: Think about this for a minute: Chinese parents living in city apartments, surrounded by gadgets and comfort, will spend thousands of yuan to send their
articles.body: Think about this for a minute: Chinese parents living in city apartments, surrounded by gadgets and comfort, will spend thousands of yuan to send their kids somewhere rural. No Wi-Fi, no phones, definitely no air-conditioning. Instead, the kids spend their summer sweating in cow sheds, hauling firewood, cleaning up after livestock. The idea behind it is as unusual as the activities themselves: parents want their children to experience hardship so they learn to appreciate the comfortable lives they have grown up with.Now, the idea sounds harsh, but there’s a method behind it. These ‘chi ku’ camps, which literally means ‘eat bitterness’, promise to teach children tougher lessons than any classroom: discipline, gratitude, and a sense of independence.Per the South China Morning Post, by summer 2026, these hardship camps were trending big time, especially as videos of homesick, teary-eyed kids circulated online. Most campers are between six and sixteen years old, as the programmes promise to teach discipline, independence, gratitude and resilience through manual labour and a temporary departure from urban comforts. Parents fork out anywhere from 5,000 yuan (approximately US$700) for ten days to over 10,000 yuan for a month. And while it started with a few adventurous families, now it’s a heated national debate: is struggling on a farm really the best way to build resilience?'Chi ku': What exactly are China's hardship camps?For starters, chi ku isn’t some new-age experiment. The phrase “eat bitterness” is deeply woven into Chinese culture: it’s the belief that going through tough times can shape character and help people appreciate what they have. Although similar programmes have existed since the early 2000s, their popularity surged during the summer of 2026. These camps take that philosophy and serve it up to urban kids who are used to city comforts, often in rural regions like Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou, where children are temporarily immersed in agricultural life.Most camps are run by private companies, not schools. Their pitch? Strip away the luxuries and plunge the kids into country life. Kids wake up early, pick tea leaves, dig potatoes, chop wood, scrub cow stalls, and if they don’t finish chores, there’s no swapping them for snacks or screen time. Some camps make them cook for themselves, old-style, over an earthen stove, with barely any seasoning.What do children do at these camps?The activities in these camps are designed to replicate the everyday responsibilities of farming families, often under physically demanding conditions.Take the ‘Swapped Lives’ camp, for example, run by Haoshi Study Tours deep in the Zhejiang mountains. For six days, nine- to twelve-year-olds work alongside local farmers, gathering firewood for hours just to cook a quick meal. According to CNA, children can spend three to four hours gathering, bundling and carrying firewood in baskets, only to use it to prepare a meal that takes around 10 minutes to eat. They also pick tea leaves, which can be exchanged for food supplies donated to disadvantaged families. In fact, picking tea leaves isn’t just an activity; it’s currency, exchanged for supplies that go to poor families. Cleaning cow stalls? Just ten to twenty minutes, but the dung becomes fertilizer or fuels biogas. One particularly grueling challenge is having kids carry a kilo of rice up a mountain before eating simple rice outside an abandoned school.How much do China's hardship camps cost?Despite the rustic setup, the camps don’t come cheap. Ten days costs around 5,000 yuan (about US$700); month-long stays push past 10,000 yuan. Kids bunk together, with six to eight of them in every room, in basic beds. Phones? Taken away upfront. Camps operate on a points system: complete tasks, earn credits, exchange for food and toiletries. Sometimes, if you don’t rack up enough points, you eat plain potatoes for dinner. That’s led critics to question whether genuine hardship is getting muddled with punishment.Why are Chinese parents sending their children to hardship camps?Mostly, they worry their kids are too spoiled. Many grew up scraping by, and now their children have everything: private schools, enrichment classes, endless tech, comfortable homes. But there’s a real concern: will these kids know how to handle life’s curveballs?Tong Lu, founder of Haoshi, said that children today don’t really grasp what it takes to earn a living or make a meal. Past generations remember hardship, as many parents and grandparents survived times when food and warmth were rare. They credit those trials for building resilience, and now fear a cushy upbringing makes their own kids soft.Is the ‘hardship camp’ too hard on kids?The emotional side of the ‘chi ku’ culture isn’t subtle either. Videos show kids crying over chopped wood, dragging heavy loads, or begging to go home. One boy complained his Shanghai parents shelled out for a plane ticket just so he’d work on a farm. Another pleaded with his mom to let him come back and study instead.It’s important to note that not everyone hates the experience; some grow comfortable with chores, and camps try to ease homesickness with parent-written letters.But all the tears and drama raise questions: are the kids ready for this level of challenge? Do hardship camps really build resilience? Psychologists warn that suffering alone doesn’t guarantee resilience. Setoh Peipei, head of psychology at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, told CNA that kids get stronger when adults help them through manageable difficulties, not when they’re simply tossed into tough situations. Desiree Qin Baolian from Michigan State University points out that a camp might help one child, but another could be traumatized. Short-term obedience isn’t the same as real emotional growth.In the end, chi ku camps shine a light on a deeper dilemma. Parents genuinely want their kids to grow tough, but there’s a fine line between teaching responsibility and making childhood needlessly hard. Sure, chores and cooking teach independence. But resilience isn’t something you can buy, package up, and deliver in a week of sweaty labor. Kids need chances to struggle, but they also need adults who’ll have their backs when things get too rough.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
articles.summary: Experts warn that using AI to enhance property images can go too far and mislead prospective buyers.
articles.body:
Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?

Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.

From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.

But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".

Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.

But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.

"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."

For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.

It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.

But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.

"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."

All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.

Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.

It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.

According to a recent survey of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.

Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.

He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.

But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.

"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."

He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.

Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.

In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.

In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.

Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.

"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.

A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".

"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."

Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.

But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.

Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.

He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.

"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

articles.title: Ankle injuries are more common than you think - here's how to protect yours
articles.summary: Performance physiotherapist Genevieve Taiwah shares her top tips for looking after your ankles.
articles.body:
They are the body's primary shock absorber, vital for balance, standing, walking and running, but most of us rarely think about our ankles - until we hurt them.

These painful incidents are very common, says Genevieve Tawiah, a performance physiotherapist who has worked on shows like Strictly Come Dancing.

Ankle injuries account for 5% of visits to A&E in the UK, according to NICE .

But Tawiah tells What's Up Docs? they can be avoided "if you are strong and aware of your foot and ankle and the chain that affects it". Here are three ways to strengthen your ankles:

The foundation to building strong ankles and reducing the risk of injuries is being "brain to body aware", says Tawiah - meaning you can sense what movements your ankles are making without relying on looking down at them.

"It's about sending information from the brain down to our foot and ankle to ground us and build a good foundation for any exercise training that follows," she says.

To build brain body awareness Tawiah has some examples of exercises that require you to watch your foot while you do them.

She suggests starting with smaller movements of the toes as this can affect how we "load [weight] through the ankles". Two examples are:

Pressing the tip of your big toe into the floor, holding it and watching how the arch of your foot engages. "This will feel like something pulling through the arch of your foot," she says.

Putting a pen on the floor next to, and parallel with, your big toe. Then try to move the big toe towards the pen, which is called toe "abduction".

Tawiah says the function of the ankle is to help us balance, weight bear and transmit force.

Heel raises - Stand next to a sturdy surface and lift your heels off the floor and roll onto your toes, making sure your ankles don't wobble or stick outwards.

Balance - Walk with one foot in front of the other, like a gymnast along a beam, and maintain your foot control.

Control - Moving from a sitting to a standing position on one or two legs and going up or down stairs are also examples of exercises used to improve ankle balance and control.

"If you go up the stairs and you find that you lead with one leg, practice leading with the other side."

Those recovering from ankle sprains might want try to balancing on one leg while throwing and catching a ball. Or work on their landing control by stepping to either side and balancing on the landing leg.

And for those with tendinopathy, chronic pain in the tendon, a slow and heavy load is important. Try calf raises with weight - for instance on a leg press.

Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles.

"A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps, pointy shoes or trainers that are narrower at the front.

"It's just worth imagining if the top of the shoe was off, would your toes have space or would your big toe be pushing over?

"Barefoot shoes are becoming increasingly popular - and can be useful - but it is important to have a good baseline of foot/ankle strength first and pace yourself with using them."

She also recommends looking for "a degree of arch support" as it affects how you take weight through your foot during a task.

She says different activities require different shoes.

"If you're doing squat exercises, you're probably going to want a flatter shoe. If you've got a spongy-soled shoe, it's going to be harder to balance and take the weight in the right place.

"Whereas if you are running, a trainer that provides more cushioning for impact or shock absortion might be more appropriate."

For longer all-terrain walks "hiking boots are often useful in reducing the risk of big sprains. However, wearing them for long periods day to day can cause increased ankle stiffness as it limits ankle mobility to a degree."

articles.title: Russell Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says ex inmate
articles.summary: The disgraced entertainer was sentenced to 10 years and six months for rape and sexual assault.
articles.body:
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.

Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.

He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.

Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.

"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."

Wandsworth prison is by far the worst I've visited

The Russell Brand I saw in court was not the flamboyant character most people will know

A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there was "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival.

"Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done.

"We're very aware of that feeling," they said.

Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle depending on where in the prison he is housed.

On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing, and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who've been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size".

The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. According to the charity, Prison Reform Trust, this is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop.

Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, inmates said.

"Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain, if he wanted.

Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC there are a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries.

They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault from mixing with other inmates.

Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences he has been convicted of could make him a target among other inmates.

Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed.

"This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved."

The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and have to go through the system to be signed off.

Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications.

"There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." He said it took five weeks to see his young son.

It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison.

At this stage nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

articles.title: Ethiopia's Tigray conflict: Has Abiy Ahmed defeated the TPLF?
articles.summary: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
articles.body:
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.

"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.

After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.

"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.

Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."

Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.

But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.

Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.

Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.

Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.

"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."

Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.

Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.

Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.

He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."

The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.

It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.

Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.

Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.

"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.

Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.

The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.

As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.

Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.

Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.

Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.

However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.

Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."

He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.

Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.

What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."

While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."

In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF . However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.

"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."

Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.

Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.

In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.

"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.

Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.

Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.

However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.

In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.

"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

articles.title: Suspect in Washington, D.C., gym shooting was doctor in legal feud with condo board
articles.summary: A doctor who was locked in a lengthy legal dispute with his condominium association after alleging his penthouse suffered mold and water damage costing him hundreds of thousands of dollars is suspected of opening fire Thursday morning at a Washington, D.C., gym.
articles.body: A doctor who was locked in a lengthy legal dispute with his condominium association after alleging his penthouse suffered mold and water damage costing him hundreds of thousands of dollars is suspected of opening fire Thursday morning at a Washington, D.C., gym. One person was killed and multiple others were injured as the rampage unfolded in the trendy Logan Circle neighborhood, just a mile from the White House, drawing a rapid law enforcement presence. The suspect, Dr. Matt Lambert, was found inside his condo at the Metropole, a seven-story luxury building, dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, officials said. The gunfire erupted just after 8 a.m. at the VIDA fitness center, located on the street level at the Metropole. A man on a treadmill said that when he heard the first bang he thought it was a popped exercise ball. Another witness told NBC News that he also heard a loud noise and saw a person in a chair fall with “blood coming from his head.” A fire alarm went off and panicked patrons raced for the exit; several fled to a nearby bagel shop to shelter in place. A federal law enforcement official and a local law enforcement official told NBC News that the suspect had gone to the gym to target a specific person; he left others unharmed. He then walked out and sprayed bullets before returning to his unit and barricading inside, the officials said. From his apartment’s balcony, the district’s interim police chief said, the gunman struck four people who were on ground level. He also fired shots into the hallway through the door before turning the gun on himself, according to officials. Building manager James Stuart, 46, of northwest Washington, D.C., was killed in the shooting, according to Jeffery Carroll, the interim chief of the Metropolitan Police Department. Carroll said that three of the survivors of the shooting rampage had “non-life-threatening injuries,” while a fourth was in critical condition. “We do know that there has been an ongoing dispute between the suspect in this case and the building, condo, homeowners association management regarding maintenance issues, mold and the like,” the interim chief told reporters at an afternoon briefing. “That there was a civil case that he filed against them. So we believe that it’s related to that.” The attorney representing Lambert in the legal case involving the condo association said Stuart was a “central fact witness” in that case. “He was also very pivotal in relaying information to the [apartment housing] board, I believe,” the lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, told reporters Thursday evening. Lawsuit alleges condo damage Lambert, 55, had been engaged in litigation with the Metropole Condo Association and EJF Real Estate Services Inc., the building’s property manager. In a March 2025 complaint filed in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia and amended in July, Lambert alleged water damage to his seventh-floor unit was the result of façade remediation that reached the complex’s northeast corner, where his condo is, in 2024. Property records show he purchased the unit for more than $1 million in 2016. From March 2024 to August 2024, Lambert said in the complaint, EJF and its engineering consultant conducted at least three leak-testing and investigatory procedures over “recurring water intrusion” into his unit. The property manager had the opportunity to identify, disclose and remediate the “ongoing moisture intrusion,” according to the complaint. Workers had even cut into the unit’s drywall to determine whether water was running behind the wall and collecting excess moisture, the suit said. Lambert alleged there was visible mold, also detectable by smell, and said he had gotten two independent assessments completed. Despite findings “confirming elevated moisture conditions, mold growth and water intrusion,” Lambert added, Metropole and EJF “failed to implement appropriate corrective action sufficient to remediate the conditions.” At a meeting in October 2024, Lambert alleged that an EJF representative dismissed his concerns and said the odor from the mold “smelled like cologne.” The lack of action led Lambert to hire his own workers to mitigate the mold contamination, he said in his suit. The situation grew so bad, he said in his filing, that it caused damage in excess of $300,000 and led to the “loss of use and enjoyment of his home.” Pictures included in his complaint showed his condo before the damage: floor-to-ceiling sweeping views of the Logan Circle neighborhood, a shrub-lined balcony and a spiral staircase. He also included pictures of what he said was the black mold uncovered in the walls and the unit left in disarray from remediation work. His lawsuit alleged gross negligence and breach of fiduciary duty, and Lambert had sought compensatory damages and related costs he said he incurred, including for inspection, testing, temporary housing, relocation and storage. The litigation was ongoing, and a remote mediation session was scheduled for March, according to court filings. Lambert’s attorney, Joel Braithwate, told reporters Thursday evening that they had spoken on Tuesday and that Lambert seemed to be in a good place as his civil case continued. The Metropole Condominium Association and EJF representatives and their attorneys did not immediately return requests for comment Thursday. The defendants denied the allegations in an answer to Lambert’s amended complaint. The condo association also filed a complaint in December 2025 naming other parties, including Urban Adventures Companies Inc., which operates the Vida fitness center, as the reason for any damage to Lambert’s unit. The complaint alleges that the gym’s dryers and a failing exhaust system “likely caused” elevated moisture levels and cites the findings of an engineering consulting firm retained by Metropole. A lawyer for VIDA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Vented on social media Lambert had regularly documented his feud with his building on social media, posting on X under the account name “OfMiceandMold.” In a post at 8:06 a.m. Thursday, he shared what he said was an engineering report about the damages to his condo, a day after he also posted pictures of the remediation work he said was necessary. “Two years of living in luxury (and the start of 6 months with no shower, dryer, HVAC, and cooking),” he stated on the account. Braithwate said Lambert, who founded a healthcare and technology consultancy company called MLEM, was in Orlando, Florida, this week for a speaking engagement and was preparing to start a new job on Monday in the medical and artificial intelligence field. He said that he never knew Lambert to be a gun owner and they had never discussed firearms. Metropolitan police said three weapons were recovered from his condo: a handgun, a rifle and a shotgun. It’s unclear how the shooter obtained the weapons, but Lambert did not have firearms registered to him in Washington, D.C., the police chief said. “We know that he used each of those firearms” on Thursday, Carroll said, adding that authorities believe “there was some level of planning associated” with the shooting rampage. Public records indicate Lambert had hunting licenses over the years in Alaska, Montana and Oregon. In one of the complaints about his condo on social media, he mentioned a new resident in April who said they had no hot water in their unit. He wrote: “If you’re looking for the building manager, I would check the gym.”

articles.title: 'Well done, specialist': Pete Hegseth awards medal to soldier who scolded his team at war memorial
articles.summary: US defence secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a military medal to the Army soldier who reprimanded him and his aides for failing to maintain silence and
articles.body: US defence secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a military medal to the Army soldier who reprimanded him and his aides for failing to maintain silence and decorum at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier during a Veterans Day visit to Arlington National Cemetery.Hegseth welcomed members of the Army unit responsible for guarding the memorial to the Pentagon on Thursday and presented Specialist Thomas Iglesias with the Joint Service Commendation Medal, the Pentagon said.The award was given "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026".Hegseth also shared photographs of the ceremony on social media, including one showing him pinning the medal on Iglesias. "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," he wrote.Soldier reminded Hegseth's team to maintain silenceIglesias drew attention after a video from Wednesday showed him reprimanding Hegseth, his wife Jennifer and several senior aides at the memorial following a Veterans Day ceremony attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.The group had taken photographs on the empty steps in front of the tomb. Laughter was heard as they spoke among themselves, prompting Iglesias to call out: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had defended the soldier's intervention after the video emerged, saying Iglesias had "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum".The Joint Service Commendation Medal is considered one of the higher military awards and is not typically given to junior enlisted service members.Hegseth faces renewed impeachment threatThe incident drew further attention to Hegseth, who survived an impeachment attempt in the House of Representatives earlier this week.The effort, led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats, was rejected in Tuesday's vote. However, Democrats, who are set to take control of both the House and Senate in January, have indicated that they could renew efforts to investigate Hegseth and pursue impeachment.At a rare Pentagon news conference on Tuesday, Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as a farce and argued that he had committed none of the high crimes required under the Constitution for his removal."This is not patriotism," he said. "This is sabotage."Hegseth has faced criticism over his handling of the Iran war, US military strikes on suspected drug vessels in Latin American waters and the dismissal of senior military officers.A memorial guarded around the clockThe Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is one of the most revered war memorials in the United States. It is the resting place of unidentified American service members, including soldiers who died in World War I, World War II and the Korean War.The site has been guarded around the clock since 1948 by soldiers from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, known as The Old Guard. articles.title: Quote of the day by Maya Angelou: “The desire to reach for the stars is ambitious. The desire to reach hearts is wise”
articles.summary: Maya Angelou was an American poet, singer, and civil rights activist. She became world-famous with her 1969 memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.
articles.body: Maya Angelou was an American poet, singer, and civil rights activist. She became world-famous with her 1969 memoir I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. She worked with Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, but beyond her work of art, her profound words of wisdom continue to resonate even today, some picked up from her own work and others from somewhere she chose to express herselfShe once said we learn early what a good life looks like, and there is nothing wrong with wanting it. Ambition gives us direction, and it gets us out of bed on difficult mornings.But do we ever look back enough at the people who shaped us?Be it a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who stayed on the phone with you at midnight. We rarely remember their achievements. We remember how they made us feel. When you think about it, that is a little strange.Maybe that is why a few short lines from Maya Angelou have travelled so far, and beautifully explain what many people take a lifetime to learn. Let us take a closer look at what she means to say.Quote of the dayThe desire to reach for the stars is ambitious. The desire to reach hearts is wiseWhat the quote meansMaya Angelou’s words, which have been widely attributed to Maya Angelou by sources like Good Reads and AtoZ Quotes, place two desires side by side. Reaching for the stars stands for ambition, including goals, success, status, and things that look impressive from far away. Reaching hearts stands for connection, meaning understanding someone, comforting them, and being remembered kindly.Angelou does not call ambition bad. She calls it ‘ambitious’, which is a fair word. But she calls the second desire wise, and this is the most profound part of his words.Ambition tells us what we want to achieve. Wisdom tells us what is worth achieving. Stars are distant and cold, while hearts are close, and that is where life actually happens. She suggests that success which never touches another person is a lonely kind of success.How are her words relevant today?We live in a time of follower counts, rankings, and performance reviews. It is easy to measure our worth in numbers. "Reach" has even become a technical term online. A post can reach a million screens and still touch no hearts.The quote reminds us that the two are not the same. A manager whom people remember is the one who listened. The teacher people thank years later is the one who believed in them. Even though machines might get better at producing words and images, the real things that hold value are only human, like kindness, attention, honesty, and warmth.You use AI every day. articles.title: U.S. officer accused of Russian spying is set to be charged in U.K., official says
articles.summary: LONDON — An American Army officer who was arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia had not handed over any information to Moscow and he is expected to be charged in Britain in the coming days, a U.S. official said Thursday.
articles.body: LONDON — An American Army officer who was arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia had not handed over any information to Moscow and he is expected to be charged in Britain in the coming days, a U.S. official said Thursday. After the British charges are filed against Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, expected on Sunday or Monday, the intention is then to prosecute him under the U.S. military justice system, the official said. No information made it into Russian hands, the official said. A second U.S. official also confirmed Tyner’s name and said he had been previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters. Tyner was a senior human resources officer and had been assigned to a NATO unit at a base near Gloucester, England. He was arrested Tuesday on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information. The Metropolitan Police announced the arrest this week and said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied that Russia has any connection to the U.S. officer. “This arrest does not concern us in any way. We don’t know what it’s connected to,” Peskov told journalists on Wednesday, according to Russian news services. “We have nothing to do with this and it has nothing to do with us.” Tyner was serving in NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester. The multinational land unit within the NATO military alliance is designed to quickly respond to crises or short-notice operations. According to the unit’s website, it is made up of forces from 20 nations but is led by the British. Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.
